citeAs: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár (2015). Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context. arXiv:1405.0312v3 [cs.CV].
creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár (Cornell NYC Tech, Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago, Facebook AI Research, Microsoft Research, Brown University, California Institute of Technology, University of California at Irvine)
description: Microsoft Common Objects in COntext (MS COCO) is a large-scale dataset for object detection and instance segmentation containing 328,000 images of complex everyday scenes with common objects in their natural context. The dataset includes 91 object categories with 2.5 million labeled instances annotated with per-instance segmentation masks. It emphasizes non-iconic images with rich contextual relationships between objects, averaging 7.7 object instances per image.
name: Microsoft COCO (MS COCO)
rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers per image for category labeling and instance spotting; 1 worker per instance for segmentation (with 3–5 workers for verification); 5 caption descriptions per image.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Worker quality on category labeling was analyzed by comparing AMT workers to 7 expert workers (co-authors). Ground truth was computed using majority vote of experts. The union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any individual expert. Worker recall saturates at around 9–10 AMT workers. It is estimated that over 99% of all object categories not later rejected as false positives are detected given 8 annotators. A leave-one-out evaluation showed workers who completed the most jobs also had the highest precision; jobs from workers below a precision threshold were rejected. For segmentation, workers below quality thresholds had all work discarded.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotation pipeline consisted of three primary stages: (1) Category Labeling — 8 AMT workers per image used a hierarchical approach grouping 91 categories into 11 super-categories; workers dragged category icons onto object instances. (2) Instance Spotting — 8 AMT workers per image placed crosses on all instances of each identified category (up to 10 instances per category per image), aided by priming from the previous stage and a magnifying glass tool. (3) Instance Segmentation — a single worker segmented each object instance using a modified OpenSurfaces interface; workers were required to pass a training task per category before annotating. Segmentations were then verified by 3–5 workers; those not receiving at least 4 of 5 favorable votes were discarded and re-queued. Workers consistently producing poor segmentations had all their work discarded. For images with more than 10–15 instances of a category, remaining instances were labeled as "crowds" using a single segment.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was explicitly designed to avoid iconic images (single large centered objects in canonical perspective) by using pairwise object/scene category queries on Flickr and applying filtering to remove iconic images. The authors note that current recognition systems perform well on iconic views but struggle with non-iconic views, and verify experimentally that models trained on MS COCO generalize better. The dataset only includes "thing" categories (not "stuff" categories like sky, grass), which may limit contextual information. The long-tail phenomenon present in other datasets (e.g., SUN) was mitigated by ensuring each category has a significant number of instances (>5,000 for 82 of 91 categories).
rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from Flickr by searching for pairs of object categories (e.g., "dog + car") and scene/object category pairs to obtain non-iconic images with rich contextual relationships. At most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded. In rare cases where enough images could not be found, single-category searches were used with an explicit filtering stage to remove iconic images. The result is a collection of 328,000 images.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images sourced from Flickr, collected by searching for pairwise combinations of object categories and scene/object category pairs. The raw images are photographs uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords.
rai:dataLimitations: The 2014 release is limited to 80 of the 91 categories; 11 categories were omitted: hat, shoe, eyeglasses (too many instances), mirror, window, door, street sign (ambiguous and difficult to label), plate, desk (confusion with bowl and dining table), and blender, hair brush (too few instances). The dataset only labels "thing" categories and not "stuff" categories (sky, street, grass), which may limit contextual information. For images with more than 10–15 instances of a category, remaining instances are marked as "crowds" and ignored during evaluation. Object category presence can be inherently ambiguous, as even expert annotators often disagree.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was split into two roughly equal halves for release (2014 and 2015). The 2014 release contains 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images (approximately 1/2 train, 1/4 val, 1/4 test). Near-duplicate images were removed and images were grouped by photographer and date to minimize cross-split duplicates. Annotations for train and validation data are released; test annotations are withheld for evaluation server use.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed (detected using GIST descriptors) and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize near-duplicates across train/val/test splits. An AMT filtering task was used to remove invalid or iconic images from candidate image sets. False positives from category labeling were handled in subsequent annotation stages.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to advance the state-of-the-art in object recognition and scene understanding, with practical applications in computer vision. Funding for all crowd worker tasks was provided by Microsoft. The dataset is designed to drive research toward more realistic, context-rich object recognition that better reflects everyday scenes.
rai:dataUseCases: Object detection, instance segmentation, semantic scene understanding, contextual reasoning between objects, precise 2D object localization, bounding box detection, image captioning, and benchmarking object recognition algorithms.

null_reasons.rai:annotatorDemographics: The paper does not describe demographics of AMT workers beyond noting they are crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not explicitly discuss missing data in the collection process beyond noting that in rare cases where enough images could not be found, single-category searches were used.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe for data collection is mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described; the dataset deals with image annotations, not missing numerical values.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: While the paper mentions the dataset will evolve and grow over time and references a 2015 release, no formal versioning or maintenance plan is described.
null_reasons.rai:machineAnnotationTools: No ML/automated annotation tools are described; annotation was performed entirely by human crowd workers on AMT. Near-duplicate detection used GIST descriptors but this was for preprocessing, not annotation.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The paper does not discuss collection of personal or sensitive information; images are of everyday scenes from Flickr.
null_reasons.license: No license is mentioned in the paper text.
